method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature) 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update' (published online 13 August 2025), 19 claims; LICENCE: © 2025 Springer Nature Limited; exclusive rights held by Springer Nature or its licensor (no open licence) (read at the article's 'Rights and permissions' section and dc.rights metadata on nature.com). S2: QUOTED from Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1) 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission' (published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242)), 14 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10837217). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference statement on diagnosis and remission criteria (Pituitary 2024, CC BY 4.0, quoted), to fill the diagnosis gap. S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. No Australian acromegaly guideline or position statement was found (Europe PMC searches for acromegaly with Australia/Australian and consensus/guideline/position statement terms). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 2 (key recommendations) add multidisciplinary-centre referral, OGTT use in diabetes and the SAGIT/ACRODAT scoring tools; the rest of Table 2 restates in-text recommendations already on the page. S2 Tables 1, 3 and 4 (ragged or merged cells) were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Diagnosis: in someone with typical features, an IGF-I above 1.3 times the upper limit of normal for age confirms acromegaly.** A fasting GH is not needed for the diagnosis. If results are equivocal, repeat IGF-I on the same validated assay; an OGTT may help. (MQ / SR / DR)
claims.source_text: In a patient with typical clinical signs and symptoms of acromegaly, IGF-I > 1.3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) for age confirms the diagnosis (MQ). GH measured after overnight fasting may be useful for informing prognosis or complications, but is not required for diagnosis (SR). However, as it is still often used as first line biochemical assessment [], a need for the use of validated GH assays worldwide is reinforced (SR). For patients with equivocal results, IGF-I measurements can be repeated using the same validated assay, and OGTT might additionally be useful (DR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Reserve the OGTT for when baseline hormones leave the diagnosis unclear.** Give 75 g glucose after fasting and measure GH at 30, 60, 90 and 120 min. BMI-based nadir cut-offs can be considered: below 0.4 µg/L if BMI is under 25, below 0.2 µg/L if BMI is 25 or more (assay dependent). Stopping oral oestrogen 4 weeks before may avoid a falsely high nadir. (SR / DR)
claims.source_text: Thus, the consensus recommended that this test be reserved for patients in whom baseline hormone levels do not clarify the diagnosis (SR). … If OGTT is performed, 75 g glucose should be administered after fasting [], and GH nadir assessed after 30, 60, 90, and 120 min [] (SR). BMI-based GH nadir cutoffs can be considered for diagnosis, with < 0.4 µg/L for BMI < 25 kg/m2 and < 0.2 µg/L for BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2 [], although this may be assay dependent (DR). As healthy premenopausal females on estrogen-containing OC have higher GH nadirs [], cessation of oral estrogen therapy 4 weeks prior to OGTT may avoid its effects on the GH axis.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Know the assay:** reference ranges differ between IGF-I immunoassays, and a high BMI lowers IGF-I for age. Use the same well-validated IGF-I assay for every assessment, and interpret new rises allowing for pregnancy, oestrogen, starvation and metabolic change. (MQ / SR)
claims.source_text: normal reference ranges are specific to each immunoassay, with the greatest differences seen at the highest values … However, body mass index (BMI) might influence normal IGF-I ranges, such that patients with high BMI have lower IGF-I levels for their age group … For all patients, ideally, the same well-validated IGF-I assay should be used for all assessments (SR). New or persistent elevations in IGF-I levels should be interpreted within the context of the individual clinical scenario and account for factors that could affect results such as pregnancy, estrogen use, starvation, and metabolic changes (SR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Measure IGF-I in every newly found pituitary mass,** and consider it for people with classic features (acral enlargement, facial and bite changes), especially with unexplained sleep apnoea or ventricular hypertrophy. Diagnosis is typically delayed 5–10 years or more, which raises comorbidity and mortality and lets the adenoma invade. (SR / DR / HQ)
claims.source_text: there may be a delay of 5-10 years or more between first symptom onset and diagnosis [, ] (HQ) … All patients with a newly diagnosed pituitary mass should undergo IGF-I measurement (SR). Although widespread screening in the general population is not warranted, IGF-I screening could be considered in individuals with classical signs, symptoms, and comorbidities of acromegaly (DR), including acral enlargement and orofacial changes, particularly if these occur in conjunction with unexplained systemic manifestations such as sleep apnea or ventricular hypertrophy
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Pituitary MRI at diagnosis for everyone:** gadolinium-enhanced, high resolution (1.5T or 3T), T1 and T2 sequences, 2–3 mm slices, reporting invasion by modified Knosp grade. Refer an equivocal microadenoma to an experienced neuroradiologist. (SR)
claims.source_text: Gadolinium-enhanced pituitary MRI should be performed in all patients at diagnosis using high-quality, high-resolution equipment, such as 1.5T or 3T scanners, where available, including T1- and T2-weighted fast spin echo sequences, with coronal and sagittal planes in 2-3 mm slice thickness with no or minimal spacing (SR). Reporting should be standardized, and include information on invasion into surrounding structures based on modified Knosp grade [] (SR). … equivocal diagnosis of acromegaly associated with pituitary microadenomas should be referred for review by an experienced neuroradiologist [] before considering further imaging studies (SR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Consider referral to a multidisciplinary pituitary centre** when biochemistry, pathology or imaging is equivocal at diagnosis, or when the response to standard treatment is insufficient. (S2 Table 2)
claims.source_text: [Table 2 row 1] Overall: Referral to a multidisciplinary pituitary center should be considered for patients with equivocal biochemical, pathology, or imaging findings at diagnosis, and for patients insufficiently responsive to standard treatment approaches.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The OGTT is safe with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes;** in uncontrolled diabetes, read both random and post-OGTT GH with caution. (S2 Table 2)
claims.source_text: [Table 2 row 14] Overall: OGTT can be safely performed among patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes mellitus. However, in patients with uncontrolled diabetes, both random and post-OGTT GH levels should be interpreted with caution.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Surgery (transsphenoidal adenoma resection) is the preferred first-line treatment**, controlling the disease in roughly 50% of patients in referral centres; about half of those who then need medical therapy reach IGF1 control.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The biochemical target of medical therapy is a normal IGF1 for age**, using the reference range for the specific assay (and a sex-specific range in puberty). (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After surgery, remission is shown by a GH nadir below 1 ng/ml on OGTT**, or below 0.4 ng/ml with modern ultrasensitive assays. Check basal and OGTT GH and IGF1 at 3 months after surgery. (DR / SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Even when controlled, keep checking GH/IGF1 for 5 years or more after surgery**, because residual tumour or relapse can occur. In year one, IGF1 every 3–6 months, then every 6–12 months.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Manage comorbidities regardless of biochemical control:** hypertension, diabetes, osteoarthrosis and sleep apnoea often persist in a sizeable share of controlled patients.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 defines surgical success as a normal IGF-I 12 weeks after surgery,** with early random GH (days 1–14) against the pre-operative level as a guide to how much adenoma was removed. If SRL was given before surgery, repeat at 3–6 months to confirm remission. In clinically controlled patients, an IGF-I in the mid to upper half of the age range may avoid inducing GH deficiency. (SR / DR / HQ)
claims.source_text: IGF-I levels should be measured 12 weeks after surgery to determine postoperative biochemical remission (SR). As the magnitude of GH decrease in the immediate postoperative period likely reflects the degree of success in adenoma removal, early random GH assessment on day 1-14 and comparison with preoperative GH levels can inform the degree of adenoma removal and subsequent longer-term remission (DR). OGTT assessment may provide further predictive value (DR). As preoperative SRL, used in patients with risk factors for more adverse surgical outcomes [], may have carryover effects that continue to influence postoperative IGF-I values [] (MQ), assessment should be repeated at 3-6 months to confirm remission (DR). … Maintaining serum IGF-I level in the mid to upper half of the age-related reference range could be considered in clinically controlled patients to avoid induction of GH deficiency [] (HQ).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs: octreotide, lanreotide) are the first-line medical option**, mostly as adjuvant treatment for active disease after surgery; primary SRL therapy suits selected patients who decline or cannot have surgery. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cabergoline alone is only for mild disease** (IGF1 below 2.0–2.5 × ULN) or mixed GH–prolactin adenomas; watch for valvulopathy and impulse-control disorders at very high long-term doses. (DR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pegvisomant alone can be first line** when glucose metabolism is badly impaired and the tumour mass is not a concern, especially where poor SRL response is expected (T2-hyperintense adenoma, very high IGF1).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check IGF1 after the first three monthly SRL injections**, ideally just before the next dose, then titrate dose or interval to IGF1. For oral octreotide capsules, check IGF1 after 2–4 weeks to titrate. (SR / DR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Surgery, not medical therapy, when there is visual loss with optic chiasm compression.** (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Switch drug class when control is not reached at maximum tolerated doses, or with adverse events;** if one drug fails, a two-drug combination of different classes is suggested. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **When a single SRL is not enough, low-dose SRL plus weekly pegvisomant is both highly effective and more cost-effective** than higher doses or more frequent dosing of either drug (S2). Pasireotide may shrink residual adenoma more than octreotide or lanreotide. (MQ / DR)
claims.source_text: For patients demonstrating insufficient control on single-agent adenoma-targeting SRL, the addition of a peripherally targeting GH receptor antagonist could be beneficial; in such cases, the combination of low-dose SRL plus weekly pegvisomant is both highly effective and more cost-effective than higher doses or more frequent dosing of these agents [] (MQ). … Pasireotide might have a more effective shrinkage effect than octreotide and lanreotide [] and may be indicated in patients with clinically relevant residual adenoma mass (DR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Higher-dose SRL regimens (off label) can help SRL-sensitive patients:** lanreotide 180 mg every 28 days or 120 mg every 21 days, or octreotide LAR 60 mg every 28 days or 30 mg every 21 days.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pegvisomant monotherapy may be the preferred second line with pre-existing hyperglycaemia or diabetes;** SRL plus pegvisomant suits partial SRL responders, and controls IGF1 in 80–96%. (DR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pasireotide LAR is an option for inadequately controlled disease**, especially with a relevant or growing adenoma and low hyperglycaemia risk; over half of patients on it develop hyperglycaemia or diabetes, so check fasting glucose and HbA1c routinely on any SRL. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If medical therapy fails, consider stereotactic radiosurgery or repeat surgery;** reserve temozolomide and other chemotherapy for aggressive or malignant tumours, under neuro-oncology.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pegvisomant: test liver function before starting and during titration, and stop it if transaminases exceed five times the upper limit of normal.** Rotate injection sites. Diabetes (especially on insulin) and obesity raise the dose needed. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **GH levels are not informative on a GH receptor antagonist** (pegvisomant): follow IGF1 instead. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pegvisomant and cabergoline: check IGF-I every 1–3 months after starting or changing the dose, then every 6–12 months;** do not measure GH on either. Injectable SRL: IGF-I 3 months after a start or dose change, then every 6–12 months once controlled. (SR)
claims.source_text: For patients who did not achieve postoperative remission and who are treated with adjuvant SRL, IGF-I should be assessed 3 months after initiation/dose adjustment of injectable SRL and 2-4 weeks after initiation/dose adjustment of oral SRL to establish an optimal dosing regimen [], and then every 6-12 months thereafter once biochemical control is achieved (SR). Random GH might be helpful in select cases where evaluation of adenoma behavior is a concern (DR). As pegvisomant and cabergoline have a shorter half-life than injectable SRL, IGF-I should be assessed every 1-3 months after treatment initiation/dose adjustment to establish the dosing regimen, and then every 6-12 months thereafter. GH assessment is not informative in follow-up of pegvisomant and cabergoline and should not be performed (SR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **After radiotherapy, medical therapy bridges until the radiation works;** once IGF-I is stable in range, pause treatment at least once a year to test for radiation-induced remission. (SR / DR)
claims.source_text: In patients receiving radiotherapy to the residual/recurrent mass, medical therapy is used as a bridge until radiation effect is seen []. In these patients, IGF-I should be assessed at the intervals appropriate for the medical therapy used (SR). With sustained decline of IGF-I within the target range, treatment can be paused at least once each year depending on rapidity of the IGF-I decline to test for the onset of radiation-induced remission (DR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **MRI 6 months after starting or switching medical therapy;** otherwise routine MRI is not needed on an SRL with controlled hormones, but image promptly for visual or eye-movement symptoms. Rapid growth or a rising largest diameter means resistance and a change of strategy. (SR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2's MRI schedule:** MRI 3–6 months after surgery as the baseline; then only for biochemical or clinical progression or when a change of modality is considered (such as before repeat surgery or radiotherapy). Regular MRI is not needed for everyone. (SR)
claims.source_text: Therefore, regular MRI follow-up is not indicated for all patients with acromegaly (SR). … MRI should be performed at 3-6 months postoperatively and used as baseline for further assessments (SR). Thereafter, MRI should be performed upon signs of biochemical or clinical disease progression, and when a change in therapeutic modality is considered, such as prior to a second surgery or radiotherapy (SR).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The SAGIT and ACRODAT scoring tools may help track disease severity and progression over time;** a prospective study of ACRODAT's clinical benefit as a monitoring tool is under way. (S2 Table 2)
claims.source_text: [Table 2 row 59] Overall: SAGIT and ACRODAT may be useful in current clinical practice for assessing changes in acromegaly disease severity and progression over time. A prospective study measuring a clinically beneficial effect of ACRODAT as a monitoring tool is underway.
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No routine gallbladder ultrasound or ECG is needed on SRLs,** but take care with other QT-prolonging drugs. (DR)
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Melmed S, di Filippo L, Fleseriu M, et al.), Nature Reviews Endocrinology (Springer Nature), 'Consensus on acromegaly therapeutic outcomes: an update', published online 13 August 2025, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-025-01148-2, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cancer screening:** there was no consensus on colonoscopy for everyone at diagnosis; UK gastroenterology guidance suggests regular screening from age 40. Screen for other cancers, including thyroid, as for the general population. (MQ)
claims.source_text: Guidelines for screening high-risk patients from the British Society of Gastroenterology and Association of Coloproctology for Great Britain and Ireland suggest regular screening beginning at age 40, and individualized considerations for repeat colonoscopy according to evidence of acromegaly disease activity and prior colonoscopy findings []. Nevertheless, there was no consensus at this Workshop on whether colonoscopy should be performed in all patients at diagnosis of acromegaly regardless of age, despite the discretionary recommendation in previous consensus publications []. For all other cancers with reported increased frequency in acromegaly, including thyroid cancer, there was consensus that screening be performed according to national/regional guidelines for the general population []. … Although acromegaly patients are at increased risk for colon cancer, increased rates of cancer-specific mortality have not been shown [] (MQ).
claims.locator: Acromegaly Consensus Group (Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, Fleseriu M, Mortini P, Strasburger C, van der Lely AJ, Wass J, Melmed S), 14th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, Pituitary 27:7-22 (doi 10.1007/s11102-023-01360-1), 'Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission', published 3 November 2023 (issue 2024; funding-statement correction PMC10837242), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10837217/, retrieved 2026-09-24
